High Tide | Engineering, costs and judge defence

This brief ties the physical response and biochemical research together for ENEC’s Advanced Technology Pioneers challenge. The system starts with the existing offshore alert. It evaluates a possible path away from seawater intake flow, runs a physical diversion within tested limits, and verifies where the animals go. A separate, contained research program asks whether a chemical cue can improve clearance. The cue would enter a later decision only if it improves measured outcomes and clears selectivity and containment gates.

Claim What is in hand Next evidence
A team can compare operating decisions and failure cases High Tide v1.0 deterministic simulator, 165 archived runs, selectable control modes and a CSV export. Reproduce laboratory water and surrogate trajectories before adjusting model coefficients.
A physical corridor can plausibly use local flow Published field and flume experiments on other jellyfish and settings. Compare matched, instrumented channel tests including a passive guide, active bubbles, distributed flow and no actuation.
The target can be guided by a chemical cue Chemical-side preference reported in other medusae. The lead molecule altered contact feeding in Japanese sea nettles. Verify local species and measure sustained directional response against water drift, followed by selectivity and fate studies in containment.
Barakah suitability Public construction, historical marine observations and modeling context. Operator-provided geometry, intake and bloom records, permissions and a viable exit.

Translate site conditions into a design envelope

The marine approach is the first study zone because it can provide time and space for sideways clearance. An intake-side structure may help shape the route or create a dead end. A channel trial would need operator review of minimum flow, maintenance access, navigation, equipment retrieval and consequences of a fault. A contained flume is the first physical test location.

Field input What to request What it changes
Geometry Permitted coarse plan, depths by datum and tide, approach cross-sections, bed, anchors and candidate routes out. Diffuser length, deployment depth, corridor shape and clearance time.
Current and waves Speed and direction at multiple depths near approach and exits, percentile and reversal duration, winds and wave window. Seasonal and reversal presets, when to run and how far a jelly can move.
Actual plant duty Hourly operating flow ranges, pump-state bands, priority channels and protected water-supply limits. Request ranges that can be shared. Intake capture assumptions and stop thresholds. The published design maximum is context only.
Bloom load Dated wet mass, collection basis, hourly or shorter bins, observer coverage, uncollected fraction, morphotypes, sizes and depths. Arrival scenarios, mass balance and whether a peak came as a sustained front or short pulse.
Return path Drifter or approved particle-tracking runs across wind and tide, discharge influence and ecological receptors. Whether an apparent release meets the clearance definition.
Marine work Seasonal restrictions, navigation, maintenance logistics, water-quality and wildlife monitoring, relevant permits. Candidate site, operating window, recovery plan and trial acceptance.
Historical response Methods, labor hours, response delay, collection and disposal volumes, observed failure modes. Baseline for economics and the decision to proceed or pivot.

The first request to ENEC can be a coarse site sketch plus de-identified ranges. A combined dataset would ideally contain timestamp, source, location_class, depth_datum, current_u, current_v, depth, wave, temperature, salinity, intake_state, wet_mass_kg, measurement_basis, species_confidence, weather, and response_state. Store missing as null, document the clock and units, and record coverage so missing data does not imply no bloom.

Calculations the judges can inspect

  1. Load window. wet kg/s = 1,000 × tonnes / (3,600 × hours). For 200 assumed metric wet tonnes, the mentor-reported daily benchmark, 24 h is 2.31 kg/s, 6 h is 9.26 kg/s, and 2 h is 27.78 kg/s. For the 300 t margin case, the corresponding rates are 3.47, 13.89 and 41.67 kg/s. Wet catch mass is not total offshore arrival. If mass is estimated from counts, use a measured distribution of individual drained wet mass and report uncertainty.
  2. Time to reach the exit. A screening approximation is t = L/u and v_side = y/t, where L is available downstream travel, u is mean along-flow speed and y is lateral travel. Over an illustrative 50 m reach with a 10 m side exit, increasing along-flow from 0.05 to 0.30 m/s cuts available time from 1,000 to 167 s and increases required mean net sideways speed from 0.01 to 0.06 m/s. This simple geometry needs measured flow and trajectories.
  3. Wet load from a transect. An initial estimate is rate = ∫ c × u_n × dA, with local wet biomass density c and water velocity normal to the cross-section u_n. Separate cross-sectional sample uncertainty, species-specific swimming and accumulation at the screens. Report intervals instead of false precision.
  4. Mass accounting. Use common tracking rules for arrivals, intake entries, outside at the final sample, retained, and other boundaries. Count returns separately because they can overlap final outcomes. In the field, define “cleared” as passing a surveyed clearance line with a follow-up check for recirculation. A simulation boundary is only a proxy.
  5. Pressure at depth. p_gauge ≈ ρgh + line losses + diffuser losses. For assumed seawater density 1,025 kg/m³, 5.5 m and 9.5 m water columns give roughly 55 and 96 kPa of static gauge head before losses. Public dredged bed elevations are relative to MSL. Actual water level and selected depth supply the real head. Request compressor curves, duty cycles and commissioning measurement before sizing.
  6. Thermal scale. P = ρ c_p Q ΔT. At 1 m³/s, 1 °C costs approximately 4.09 MW thermal before losses using assumed seawater properties. At the published 690 m³/s design scenario, the arithmetic is around 2.82 GW thermal per °C. Study thermal preferences in containment and use temperature as a seasonal predictor. Open-water heating is outside the concept.
  7. Chemical scale. The chemistry dossier compares the arithmetic for a contained loop and an aggregate design-flow example. This illustrates dilution and inventory. No waterborne concentration has been established as effective or safe for the target.
  8. Cost and energy. Convert actual electrical power and duty to kWh before comparing energy. The simulator’s actuation index is an internal relative metric. Derive any predicted savings from observed labor and avoided service work at comparable load, and include inspection and replacement. An unmeasured outage cost or avoided outage should stay outside the ROI calculation.

Air demand and compressor sizing

The mentors asked how much air we would need. The answer depends on the length active at once, diffuser depth, pressure loss, and the air rate that actually produces a usable lateral flow. Request free-air delivery at working pressure from suppliers, with flow reference temperature and pressure stated. A nominal displacement or receiver volume alone does not size a compressor.

A published bubble-plume basin experiment measured a 0.55–1.67 L/s per metre range at normalized pressure. It is an order-of-magnitude reference for testing a plume. Effectiveness for jellyfish at Barakah requires a separate test. For a candidate segment, multiply the tested per-metre flow by the active length. Bubble curtain basin measurements, §2.4

Illustrative active length Normalized air flow using basin reference Approximate shaft/electrical planning proxy at the assumptions below
10 m 5.5–16.7 L/s, or 0.33–1.00 m³/min 0.71–2.15 kW
40 m 22–66.8 L/s, or 1.32–4.01 m³/min 2.83–8.59 kW

These screening calculations assume 8 m water depth, 1,025 kg/m³ water, 20 kPa line and diffuser allowance, 101.325 kPa inlet, 1.4 specific-heat ratio, and 60% combined efficiency. They imply roughly 100 kPa gauge delivery pressure. The ideal-gas compression proxy is P = γ/(γ−1) × p₁ × Q₁ × [(p₂/p₁)^((γ−1)/γ) − 1] ÷ η, with absolute pressures and intake-referenced airflow. The illustrative calculation treats normalized flow as intake-referenced for this scale comparison. Confirm air temperature/reference conversion, leakage, wet/fouled losses, pressure drop to the farthest segment, redundancy, acoustic effects and duty cycle before selecting equipment. A vendor performance curve and measured plume are the sizing gates.

For the first bench run, meter air at each active section. Record depth, inlet and manifold pressures, flow balance, angle, wave proxy, water trajectories and exit fraction. Map the settings that give clearance. More air can change the flow pattern or even increase crossing under some wave conditions. A higher airflow reading alone does not establish better diversion. Haberlin et al., field and flume comparison

Deployment logic and acceptance

  • Observe. Confirm the incoming bloom, watch the exit and measure local conditions. The operator retains control and uses current procedures.
  • Select. Test a verified route against the live flow direction and accepted operating range. Approve one physical mode for the envelope and keep a safe fallback.
  • Actuate and monitor. Stage removable segments where appropriate. Check that upstream retention does not grow and that the outside route clears at a rate that holds under sustained arrival.
  • Stop and escalate. Unavailable exit, unacceptable return, loss of water supply margin, equipment fault or effects outside agreed welfare limits stop the trial. Recovery and removal should be possible without interrupting existing screens or plant operation.

During mentoring, ENEC described trash-rack removal as a current response and highlighted jellyfish survival. Use rack-side handling as the reference if the operator can provide comparable data. In a qualified trial, score body condition at the exit and survival during an agreed follow-up period, rather than assuming that crossing the boundary demonstrates recovery. Keep fish and sea turtles in the non-target assessment. Use a measurement and acceptance plan jointly defined with ENEC before a marine pilot. Proposed starting comparison metrics are clearance fraction, approach-to-exit time, final intake fraction, retention at fixed times, repeat returns, contact, water-supply impact, actuator duty, inspection time, and maintenance hours. Separate biological effects from engineering performance. A provisional laboratory target might be an absolute increase of 15 percentage points in verified exits for the combined cue and physical method versus the physical method alone. A threshold that matters at Barakah must be agreed from the site’s requirements and uncertainty.

Stage budget and decision gates

All amounts below are planning allowances in AED. None is a supplier quote or a capital budget for plant installation. Cost buckets are separated to avoid adding bench hardware twice. Taxes, civil works at the plant, operational downtime, major permits and permanent equipment require separate scoping.

Stage Low High Decision before spending more
Student bench demonstrator with neutral surrogates, basic pumps, flow observation, controls and reserve 2,160 8,640 Confirm repeatable flow and tracking in both branches and reproducible physical baseline.
Contained feasibility with qualified partner, identification, care, analytical chemistry, preliminary non-target endpoints and reserve 35,625 125,000 Reproduce a directional effect, recovery and an initial selectivity window. Proceed separately from marine deployment.
Combined planning envelope for the two stages above 37,785 133,640 Refine with written quotes and partner availability. Shared items and contributions can reduce the combined cost.
Marine pilot or permanent system Quote after design Quote after design Approve survey, route, environmental study, exact work scope, operating/maintenance model and retrieval plan.

A later field work breakdown needs hydrodynamic survey and model validation, structural and mooring design, fabrication and compression or pumping equipment, instrument calibration, civil and marine installation, inspections, fouling management, power, specialist labor, seasonal demobilization and decommissioning. Ask for itemized prices, warranty, life and deliverable dates. Compare passive and active configurations on equal geometry, flow and clearance criteria.

What could a small marine pilot cost?

This is a bottom-up planning exercise for one recoverable, physical-only trial at an approved non-operational test area. The allowance assumes one installation/retrieval campaign and borrowed site access. Quantities and unit rates below are project assumptions to replace with quotations. They do not price installation at Barakah or authorization to work there.

Cost driver Low calculation High calculation
Survey planning, engineering and method review 80 h × AED 250 = 20,000 180 h × AED 450 = 81,000
Current, depth, observation and calibration equipment rental 6 days × AED 1,000 = 6,000 12 days × AED 4,000 = 48,000
Removable test hardware, fabrication and spares AED 30,000 allowance AED 100,000 allowance
Marine logistics, field team and retrieval 3 days × AED 3,500 = 10,500 6 days × AED 15,000 = 90,000
Environmental observation and verification AED 10,000 allowance AED 35,000 allowance
Data analysis and trial report AED 5,000 allowance AED 20,000 allowance
Illustrative subtotal AED 81,500 AED 374,000
Illustrative total with 30% reserve AED 105,950 AED 486,200

Price civil work, operating interfaces, permissions, specialist review, operational downtime, and taxes separately once a trial boundary exists. Keep the contained biochemical study separate. To narrow the range, secure two rental quotes, use one measured deployment footprint, and confirm available labor, power and equipment with the test partner.

For operating costs, use annual energy = measured kW × hours per event × events per year and separately estimate crew time and spares. An illustrative 15 kW, 8-hour event, 20 events per year, at AED 0.30/kWh gives 2,400 kWh and AED 720 per year for actuation energy alone. The same assumed 20 events with two people at eight hours each and AED 100/hour gives AED 32,000 in response labor. These are sensitivity inputs, not Barakah duty, tariffs or crew costs. The example shows why a real trial needs crew and maintenance logs as well as power readings.

Questions to practise aloud

Judge question A defensible answer
“What’s proprietary here?” “The components have prior art. Our engineering contribution is the integration of a tested exit, selectable actuation, continuous clearance accounting and a biochemical assay with a real decision gate.”
“Is the cue a pheromone?” “We’re testing a candidate cue. The identified molecule changed contact feeding in a different species. We still have to demonstrate directional behavior in the animals ENEC encounters.”
“Won’t other animals react?” “They might. We measure the target response and compare it with relevant non-target endpoints at verified exposures. Containment and recovery are part of the trial design.”
“Why not just catch them at the screen?” “That remains an operational baseline. We would measure whether clearing upstream reduces retained mass and handling load without moving the problem into another accumulation point.”
“Can you deal with a 200-tonne day?” “An ENEC mentor reported a historical peak around 200 tons in one day. We assume metric wet tonnes in our arithmetic and test 300 t as a 50% margin case. The same mass over two hours is twelve times the daily average rate. We need the event record and clearance geometry before making a capacity claim.”
“Does your zero-intake run prove it works?” “It shows a model behavior under stated assumptions. We need flume calibration, repeated sustained arrivals, a no-actuation comparison and an operator-agreed clearance line before making performance claims.”
“What if the power fails?” “The design premise is a fail-to-stop actuation system with the existing operator response intact. We test fault outcomes and review passive equipment, retrieval and obstruction risks before any pilot.”
“What if no route exits safely?” “That layout fails the corridor gate. We would assess a different zone or a separate collection-and-relocation concept with ENEC.”
“What would you build with AED 10,000?” “A recirculating bench demonstrator, neutral surrogates, flow and video measurements, and a documented validation dataset. A target-species chemistry study requires a qualified partner and a separate budget.”
“What would make you abandon chemistry?” “Failure to produce useful directional movement beyond flow, or evidence that recovery, selectivity, containment or operating practicality is inadequate.”
